newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Gujral clears one hurdle, but many remain.
newsitem.headline: India's Gujral clears one hurdle, but many remain.

text.p: India's three-week-old government has notched up its first victory by swiftly pushing a pathbreaking budget through parliament despite grumbling from within its ranks.
But Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral can scarcely afford to pause for breath before tackling an array of problems staring his 15-party coalition in the face, analysts said on Sunday.
"Getting the budget through was a minor victory. All the tough decisions have yet to come," said E. Sridharan, a coalition politics analyst at the Centre for Policy Research.

On Friday the Finance Bill enacting the 1997/98 budget starting in April and a raft of economic liberalisation steps, sailed through the lower house of parliament despite initial murmurs of protest from the United Front alliance's powerful communist members and opposition parties.
"It was a triumph, it is proof that economic reforms are on course, that they enjoy a great deal more support than we imagine," independent political analyst Rasheed Talib said.
"But now that the government has got the budget out of the way, it will have to get down to brass tacks," he said.

One unpleasant task that Gujral has pledged to quickly deal with is plugging India's 155 billion rupee ($4.33 billion) oil pool deficit, a drain on government resources created by the domestic sale of petroleum products at subsidised rates.
Industry analysts say a rise in oil prices is inevitable -- a move that is sure to spark strong opposition from the coalition's leftwing members and stoke inflation.

Gujral must also win over the left in order to clamp a lid on a growing subsidies bill and to press ahead with privatising loss-making state firms, both regarded as vital to cut state spending and invigorate the Indian economy.
The communists, who helped pitchfork the soft spoken prime minister into power last month, are not his only worry.
Barely in the saddle, Gujral has already been jolted by a federal police decision to prosecute the chief of his Janata Dal party in a $280 million scandal over animal fodder funds.
Party president Laloo Prasad Yadav has declared his innocence and refused to resign, further embarrassing Gujral, who enjoys an untarnished reputation for honesty.
Local news reports say Yadav has threatened to bring down Gujral's government if he presses for his prosecution.
"Mr Gujral is possibly placed in an invidious situation," Talib said. "Every way you look at it, he is facing a problem."
In addition to rumblings within his motley coalition, the prime minister might also need to deal with a fresh threat from the alliance's key ally, the Congress party, analysts said.

Sonia Gandhi, the Italian-born widow of late prime minister Rajiv Gandhi, on Thursday decided to join Congress, whose 140 deputies provide crucial support to the United Front's 178 in the 542-member lower house of parliament.
Debilitated by internal bickering and scandals, Congress suffered a crushing defeat at the polls last year.
But Talib said the elegant 50-year-old widow's entry could marshal the once mighty party that has ruled India for all but five years since independence from Britain in 1947.
"A Congress more hopeful about its chances at the hustings may make the present government a little shaky," Talib said.
"If prospects of Congress unity start improving, as they well might under Mrs Gandhi, this will obviously start making them a little more cocky."
Congress last flexed its political muscles in March, when it suddenly withdrew its support to Gujral's predecessor, H.D. Deve Gowda, and toppled him in a parliamentary confidence vote.

"Gujral's government is first and foremost a minority government and then a coalition government. That makes it weak on two counts," Sridharan said. "His short-run situation is very difficult." ($1=35.8 rupees)
